COUNCIL MEETING MINUTES – LEGISLATIVE SESSION

• President Mattscheck declared the public hearing open for the proposed 2027 City Budget at 7:32pm. 
• Finance C hairman Mr. Bronner summarized the budget, noting: 
o Tax revenues are expected to remain relatively flat in 2026 with modest growth in 2027. 
o State and local government revenues were conservatively budgeted. 
o Charges for services, permits and fines are expected to increase slightly. 
o General Fund revenues for 2027 are budgeted at approximately $11.74 million, exceeding projected 
expenditures. 
o The Street Maintenance Fund, Capital Improvement Fund, Sewer Service Fee Fund and Fire/EMS 
Capital Improvement Fund remain financially stable. 
o One ambulance purchase is planned for 2027. 
o Recommended transfers include: 
▪ $250,000 from the Earnings Tax Fund to the Growth Fund. 
▪ $200,000 from the Stadium Fund to the General Fund. 
• During public comment, Maggie Wilson requested future funding consideration for accessibility 
improvements, including ADA access to Koenig Park and additional curb cuts around the city.

(2) Scott Knable (Department of Transportation) & Kelly Scocco (Public Service Director of the City of Columbus) 
Scott Knable of the Ohio Department of Transportation (ODOT) introduced Kelly Scocco from the City of Columbus to share
Columbus' experience with roadway safety improvements similar to those being considered for Reading. 
Scott explained that after attending a recent presentation by Kelly, he recognized many similarities between the challenges
Columbus had faced and those currently before Reading City Council. He invited Kelly to discuss several roadway improvement
projects completed in Columbus and to answer questions based on those experiences. 
Introduction 
Kelly explained that Columbus refers to these projects as road optimization rather than "road diets." 
The goal of road optimization is to make roadways as safe as possible while ensuring they function effectively for everyone who
uses them, including motorists, bicyclists, pedestrians, and public transit. 
She noted that although she had never presented to another city council before, she was passionate about roadway safety and
welcomed the opportunity to help another community navigate similar decisions. 
Indianola Avenue: The First Road Optimization Project 
In 2016, shortly after Mayor Andrew Ginther took office, Columbus proposed converting a section of Indianola Avenue from four
travel lanes to three while adding bicycle lanes.

Page 10 07-21-2026 Reading Council Minutes 
The proposal divided the community. Approximately half of the residents opposed the project, while the other half supported it
because of concerns about speeding. 
When city officials presented the proposal to the mayor, he asked a simple question: 
"Will this make the road feel like a neighborhood street rather than a raceway?" 
When staff confirmed that it would, the project moved forward. 
Although opponents strongly resisted the project during construction, the controversy disappeared once it was completed. Traffic
continued to flow smoothly, congestion never materialized, and the roadway simply functioned as intended. 
Kelly acknowledged that, at the time, even transportation professionals questioned whether reducing four lanes to three would
create congestion. Instead, drivers naturally merged into a single travel lane where appropriate, and traffic continued moving
efficiently. 
Livingston Avenue: Addressing Dangerous Speeds 
During the COVID-19 pandemic, Livingston Avenue experienced extreme speeding, with some vehicles traveling more than 70
miles per hour. 
The speeding became so severe that vehicles were crashing into homes. Residents no longer felt safe walking, biking, or even
sitting inside their own houses. 
After studying the corridor, Columbus quickly converted the roadway from four lanes to three during a resurfacing project. 
The results were dramatic: 
• Excessive speeding decreased by more than 90%. 
• Drivers continued to travel at the posted speed limit. 
• Overall crashes were reduced by 50%. 
Kelly emphasized that the objective was never to slow normal traffic below the speed limit. Instead, the design prevented
excessive speeding while maintaining efficient traffic flow. 
Mound Street 
Columbus implemented a similar road optimization project on Mound Street near an elementary school where speeding had
become a significant concern. 
Following the lane reduction: 
• Excessive speeding declined. 
• Traffic crashes decreased. 
• Safety around the school improved. 
Broad Street (U.S. Route 40) 
Broad Street originally consisted of seven lanes, including three travel lanes in each direction and a center turn lane. 
As part of Columbus' Vision Zero initiative, the city removed one travel lane in each direction. 
Vision Zero aims to eliminate all traffic fatalities on Columbus roadways by 2035. 
Kelly noted that while Columbus still recorded more than 40 roadway fatalities last year, that number had declined significantly
from a high of 72 fatalities in 2021. 
The Broad Street project produced impressive safety improvements: 
• Traffic crashes decreased by 50%. 
• Excessive speeding decreased by 91%.

Page 11 07-21-2026 Reading Council Minutes 
Protected bicycle lanes also encouraged far greater bicycle use. Within the first five months, bicycle traffic increased from
virtually none to approximately 12,000 riders. 
Most importantly, roadway safety improved for everyone—not just bicyclists, but motorists as well. 
Expanding the Success 
More recently, Columbus completed the remainder of the Indianola Avenue project through the Clintonville business district. 
Instead of bicycle lanes in some areas, on-street parking was added where appropriate. 
The neighborhood welcomed the improvements, traffic congestion did not occur, and the roadway continued to operate
effectively. 
Lessons Learned 
Kelly stressed that she was not trying to persuade Council to support or oppose any particular project. Instead, she wanted to share
Columbus' experiences and answer questions. 
She recalled that residents along Livingston Avenue feared reducing lanes would divert traffic into nearby neighborhoods. In
practice, that never happened because drivers could still travel at the posted speed limit, making alternative routes unnecessary. 
When evaluating roadway changes, Columbus focuses on several key considerations: 
• Total traffic volume. 
• Whether the roadway carries fewer than approximately 20,000 vehicles per day, a threshold where four-lane roads can
often be reduced to three lanes without creating congestion. 
• Proper intersection design, including dedicated turn lanes that allow turning vehicles to clear through traffic and maintain
efficient traffic flow. 
A Final Reflection 
Kelly concluded by sharing a story that had greatly influenced her perspective. 
Several years earlier, she attended a conference where former Hoboken, New Jersey Mayor Ravi Bhalla spoke about his city's
commitment to traffic safety. 
While serving on city council, Bhalla had voted against a major roadway redesign because of significant public opposition. 
Not long afterward, a beloved member of the community was struck and killed while walking on that same roadway. 
When Bhalla later became mayor, he committed himself to making roadway safety his highest priority, regardless of public
criticism. His guiding principle became being "unapologetic about saving people's lives." 
Kelly said that message deeply resonated with her. She closed by explaining that her reason for speaking before Reading City
Council was simple: if she truly believed in being unapologetic about saving lives, she also had a responsibility to share the
experiences and lessons that had proven successful in Columbus. 
AUDIENCE ASKING PARTICIPATION:
(1) Patrick McCarthy: thanked the City of Columbus representative for her presentation but expressed concerns about
comparing Reading to Columbus. 
He noted that Reading is a small, landlocked community of approximately 10,400 residents, while Columbus is the state capital
with significantly greater financial resources and the ability to continue expanding. Because of these differences, he questioned
whether examples from Columbus were applicable to Reading. 
Mr. McCarthy also observed that many of the examples presented were based on projects completed 10 to 12 years ago. He
recalled that previous discussions with city officials referenced an ODOT traffic count showing approximately 16,000 vehicles
per day on Reading Road. Although he acknowledged the traffic study was a few years old, he confirmed with council members
that this was the most recent figure reported by ODOT. 
Mr. McCarthy questioned the proposed conversion from four travel lanes to two travel lanes with a center turn lane.

Page 12 07-21-2026 Reading Council Minutes 
He disagreed with the suggestion that motorists could simply use the center turn lane to drive around stopped buses. In his view,
the center lane is intended solely for turning movements and cannot legally function as a passing lane. He stated that he did not
believe such a practice would be acceptable in Reading. 
Mr. McCarthy asked what financial impact the proposal would have on the City of Reading after ODOT's involvement ended. He
questioned the ongoing costs associated with: Maintaining pavement markings, traffic signals, utility expenses & general roadway
maintenance. 
Council members responded that Reading receives reimbursement from the State of Ohio for maintenance on Reading Road,
including snow removal, salt, equipment, and employee time associated with maintaining the roadway. 
Mr. McCarthy discussed bicycle opportunities within the city, noting that Reading already has parks and other locations suitable
for recreational cycling. Speaking as a cyclist himself, he stated that he has no desire to ride on busy city streets. He cited
concerns about vehicle traffic, air pollution, and motorists who fail to notice bicyclists. He questioned whether adding bicycle
accommodations to Reading Road would truly improve cyclist safety and expressed skepticism about claims regarding reductions
in fatalities without seeing supporting data. 
Mr. McCarthy voiced significant concern about how the proposed roadway changes could affect local businesses. He questioned
whether any study had been completed to evaluate the economic impact of making businesses more difficult to access.
Specifically, he expressed concern that motorists would no longer be able to make convenient turns into businesses and might
instead have to wait in the center turn lane or continue past their destination before turning around. He suggested these changes
could discourage customers from stopping at local businesses, resulting in lost revenue. 
Returning to the comparison between Reading and Columbus, Mr. McCarthy emphasized that Reading's size and geography make
it fundamentally different from a large metropolitan area. He argued that improving Reading does not necessarily require
reducing the number of travel lanes on Reading Road. Mr. McCarthy suggested that safer bicycle facilities should be located in
parks or on dedicated trails where riders of all ages can enjoy cycling away from heavy traffic. He stated that encouraging bicycle
traffic on a roadway carrying approximately 16,000 vehicles per day does not appear to be an appropriate solution. 
Mr. McCarthy concluded by expressing concern that reducing the number of travel lanes would: Increase travel times, create
additional vehicle emissions and air pollution, increase opportunities for crashes & negatively affect local businesses by reducing
accessibility. 
(2) Bob Wimmers: Began by expressing disappointment that the City of Columbus representative had left immediately after
her presentation and not allowing an opportunity to ask questions. Mr. Wimmers said he would like additional information
regarding the studies behind the proposal. Specifically, he questioned whether research had been conducted to determine: 
• How much the proposed roadway changes would slow traffic. 
• What traffic volumes are expected in five, ten, or fifteen years. 
• Whether long-term traffic projections had been considered before recommending permanent roadway changes. 
He emphasized that once the roadway is redesigned, reversing those changes would be difficult or impractical. 
Responding to an earlier comment from a council member that the community would not know the outcome until the changes
were implemented, Mr. Wimmers acknowledged that point but stressed that the decision would effectively be permanent.
Because of that, he encouraged careful consideration before proceeding with any modifications to Reading Road. 
Mr. Wimmers also questioned whether the Columbus representative had conducted any study specific to Reading before making
her presentation. He asked whether she was familiar with: Reading's business district, the City's unique traffic patterns & Major
local corridors such as Columbia Avenue and Benson Street. 
(3) Mark Haeufle: Began by observing that, based on his conversations throughout the community, the majority of residents
appear to oppose the proposed Reading Road lane reduction. He stated that whether he is at local organizations or businesses—
including the VFW, American Legion, Eagles, Foley's, Benson's, The Valley, or Gertz Pony Keg—most people he speaks with
are against the proposal. While he acknowledged that some supporters exist, he believes they are in the minority. 
Mr. Haeufle explained that, through his work loading trucks, he is familiar with roadway dimensions and agrees that the current
nine-foot travel lanes are narrower than ideal. He also acknowledged that Reading Road has legitimate safety concerns. However,

he believes the primary issue is congestion rather than lane width. He cited several factors that regularly interrupt traffic flow,
including: Stopped trains, Metro buses loading and unloading passengers & general traffic congestion 
According to Mr. Haeufle, business owners have expressed concern that reducing Reading Road to one travel lane in each
direction could significantly harm the local economy. He specifically noted that employees and patrons at Gertz Pony Keg have
repeatedly told him they believe the proposal would negatively impact the community.
While acknowledging that the proposed changes might reduce crashes on Reading Road, Mr. Haeufle questioned whether they
would simply shift traffic onto neighborhood streets. He expressed concern that motorists seeking to avoid congestion would
divert through residential areas, potentially: Increasing traffic on neighborhood streets, creating additional safety concerns for
residents and children & hindering emergency response by affecting access for police and fire vehicles. 
He also questioned whether increased congestion near City Hall and the public safety facilities could make it more difficult for
emergency vehicles to leave the station when responding to calls. 
(4) Unnamed Council Guest: Asked what plans are in place to address traffic if the proposed Reading Road lane reduction is
implemented. The resident explained that traffic on Columbia Avenue already backs up as far as Jefferson Avenue. As
congestion increases, many drivers bypass the traffic by cutting through nearby residential side streets. 
The speaker noted that residents who live along these streets have already experienced increased traffic volumes, even without the
proposed roadway changes. While acknowledging that predictions about future conditions involve some speculation, the resident
emphasized that the current traffic diversion onto neighborhood streets is a documented and ongoing issue. 
The resident expressed concern about the driving behavior already occurring on Columbia Avenue. According to the speaker,
motorists frequently accelerate aggressively between the stop sign and the traffic signal, creating conditions that resemble a drag
strip. The resident suggested that police officers could issue numerous speeding citations because of the frequency of these
violations. The speaker also reported witnessing drivers crossing into oncoming traffic lanes to pass vehicles that are traveling at
the posted speed limit. These unsafe passing maneuvers already occur where Columbia Avenue transitions into two travel lanes. 
The resident concluded by asking what specific plans the City has to address additional traffic diversion if the proposed Reading
Road lane reduction is approved. The speaker requested information on how officials intend to manage the anticipated increase in
vehicles using neighborhood streets, given that this pattern is already occurring under existing traffic conditions. 
(5) Carl Beckman: Introduced himself as a motorist rights advocate and explained that although he lives in Pleasant Ridge
rather than Reading, he has a strong interest in the community. He stated that he has followed local issues affecting Reading and
encouraged City Council to reject the proposed Reading Road lane reduction. 
Mr. Beckman explained that Reading Road serves as an important alternate route whenever nearby highways are closed. 
He noted that: 
• Interstate 75 was closed for a weekend several weeks earlier, resulting in increased traffic on Reading Road. 
• When Interstate 71 northbound is closed, he personally uses Reading Road and U.S. Route 42 to travel north to visit a
family member in Lebanon, Ohio. 
• More recently, State Route 562 (the Norwood Lateral) was closed following a fatal crash, causing traffic to divert onto
local roadways such as Reading Road. 
He expressed concern that reducing roadway capacity could make it more difficult for Reading Road to accommodate traffic
during these unexpected events. 
Mr. Beckman stated that some communities have declined to implement road diet proposals. He cited cities in Northern
Kentucky, including Florence, as examples and suggested that Reading should recognize that rejecting the proposal remains a
reasonable option. 
Mr. Beckman discussed a road diet implemented in Pleasant Ridge, where he said residents have experienced rear-end collisions
involving impatient drivers. According to his observations, drivers become frustrated when they are unable to pass slower-
moving traffic because only one travel lane is available in each direction.

Page 14 07-21-2026 Reading Council Minutes 
He explained that when driving on four-lane roads, he typically remains in the right lane and allows faster traffic to pass,
believing this reduces his risk of being struck from behind. 
Mr. Beckman recalled recent flooding in Pleasant Ridge that caused significant traffic congestion along Montgomery Road. He
noted that emergency vehicles, including those from the St. Bernard Fire Department responding to incidents in Cincinnati,
encountered difficulty navigating through the heavy traffic. He suggested that roadway capacity should remain sufficient to
support emergency response during unusual events such as severe weather. 
Mr. Beckman revisited concerns he had raised during a previous council meeting in January regarding delivery vehicles stopping
in travel lanes. At that time, snow-covered parking lanes limited available stopping space. However, he stated that even during
good weather, delivery vehicles continue to stop in the roadway rather than pulling out of traffic. He explained that this often
forces motorists to cross the centerline to continue traveling safely. 
Mr. Beckman noted that some municipalities have chosen not to adopt Vision Zero policies. He stated that information regarding
Vision Zero is publicly available and encouraged Council members to research the topic independently before making a decision. 
Mr. Beckman concluded by expressing concern about the impact of speed humps and speed tables on smaller vehicles. He
explained that he drives a Ford Escort and believes these traffic-calming devices place additional wear on his vehicle's suspension
system. He also expressed his opinion that speed humps and speed tables can slow emergency vehicles responding to calls. 
(6) Unnamed Council Guest: Began by questioning earlier comments regarding tractor-trailers turning onto neighborhood
streets, noting that such movements should not normally occur. The resident then asked whether a study had been conducted on
the number of crashes occurring along Reading Road. Council responded that the crash analysis was performed by the Ohio
Department of Transportation (ODOT) as part of its study and that the findings are included in the agency's report. 
The speaker stated that the greatest concern is not Reading Road itself, but the residential streets that connect to it. The resident
explained that these neighborhood streets are home to families and children who regularly play outside. If traffic is diverted from
Reading Road onto these side streets, the speaker believes those neighborhoods could experience significantly higher traffic
volumes and increased safety risks. 
The resident acknowledged previous comments suggesting that the community would not know the actual effects of the proposal
until it is implemented. However, the speaker expressed concern that waiting to see the outcome could have serious
consequences if the anticipated traffic diversion results in a tragic incident. The resident emphasized that if increased
neighborhood traffic were to contribute to the injury or death of a child, the community could not simply reverse the
consequences afterward. The speaker urged Council to reject the proposed Reading Road lane reduction, stating that protecting
the safety of children and preserving the character of Reading's residential neighborhoods should remain the highest priority. 
(7) Jennifer Dick: Reminded Council that she had submitted an email during the previous meeting regarding excessive speeding
on Harvest Avenue. She noted that she had already shared her views on the proposed Reading Road lane reduction and instead
wanted to focus on the continuing safety concerns in her neighborhood. She thanked Mr. Thamann for responding to her
concerns and for visiting the area to discuss the issue. 
Since that discussion, several additional incidents have occurred. An Amazon delivery truck struck and damaged a neighbor's
fence, and within the past two weeks, two vehicles were traveling at such high speeds that they struck the curb, leaving visible tire
marks. Jennifer explained that she has raised concerns about speeding on Harvest Avenue for years. While she appreciates the
newly improved roadway, she believes the smoother pavement has encouraged motorists to drive even faster. 
Jennifer described the measures she and her neighbors have taken to help protect their community. She stated that she has already
purchased several safety signs and regularly sits in a lawn chair near the roadway so neighborhood children can safely ride their
bicycles in the evenings. She also noted that another neighbor monitors traffic farther up the street. She expressed concern that, if
conditions do not improve, a child, a pedestrian, or someone walking a dog could eventually be seriously injured or killed. She
acknowledged that she herself could also be at risk while trying to slow traffic. 
Jennifer asked Council to consider reducing the speed limit on Harvest Avenue as a practical safety measure. She stated that if
the City cannot provide additional signage, she is willing to purchase it herself. However, she noted that the street does not even
have a posted 25 mph speed limit sign and asked for guidance on obtaining appropriate signs, such as a lower speed limit sign and
"Children at Play" signs, including the associated costs. 
(8) Sue Renderle: Referenced the January 28, 2026, Ohio Department of Transportation (ODOT) presentation, during which

Page 15 07-21-2026 Reading Council Minutes 
Carolyn Duffy, President of 143 Engineers LLC, presented crash statistics for Reading Road covering the previous five years.
According to the presentation, there were 949 reported crashes during that period. Of those, 10 involved pedestrians and eight
involved bicyclists, for a combined total of 18 crashes, representing approximately 1.9% of all reported crashes. The presentation
also indicated that approximately 10.9% of the crashes were identified as speed-related. Additionally, the highest recorded speed
associated with a speed-related crash was reported to be 33 miles per hour. Based on these figures, Sue questioned whether the
available crash data supports the conclusion that Reading Road has a significant safety problem requiring a road diet. 
Sue also encouraged Council to consider the potential economic effects of a road diet. She stated that many businesses along
Reading Road rely on convenient access, adequate traffic flow, and visibility to attract customers. In her view, reducing roadway
capacity could increase congestion, make businesses less accessible, and negatively affect local commerce. She asked Council
whether members had spoken directly with business owners along Reading Road to understand their perspectives on the proposed
changes. 
Sue concluded by thanking the City for implementing the TextMyGov notification system. She said it has been an effective way
to keep residents informed about important news and events happening throughout the community. 
(9) Maggie Wilson: Addressed Council regarding the importance of representation and the responsibility elected officials have
to their constituents. 
(10) Ryan Hasty: Addressed the council regarding the proposed Reading Road diet, emphasizing the importance of representing

Council discussed creating or expanding educational materials on the city's website and social media platforms. Visual 
information, including photographs showing the differences among e-bikes, dirt bikes, mini bikes, and other types of 
motorized bicycles, could help residents understand the regulations. It was indicated that some information may already be 
available on the city's website and agreed to review the existing materials to determine whether additional or clearer 
information is needed. 
Council members also referenced similar educational information recently published by police departments in neighboring 
communities, including Mariemont, Blue Ash, Evendale, and Sharonville. The information from those communities generally 
reflects the requirements of the Ohio Revised Code. 
Youth Safety and Education 
Council discussed the possibility of connecting families with organizations that offer bicycle or e-bike safety classes for 
children. Because e-bikes are becoming increasingly popular, officials agreed that safety education could be beneficial. 
However, it was explained that staffing limitations make it difficult for the city's police department to conduct its own classes 
at this time. Outside organizations or existing community programs may provide a more practical option. 
Key Takeaways 
• The city will continue reviewing e-bike classifications and applicable regulations. 
• Officials will clarify the relationship between local rules and the Ohio Revised Code. 
• Existing city website and social media information will be reviewed and expanded if necessary. 
• Educational materials with photographs and clear descriptions could help residents distinguish between different 
types of bikes. 
• Parents are encouraged to understand an e-bike's classification and legal requirements before purchasing one for a 
child. 
• Class 3 e-bikes can reach speeds of up to 28 mph and have specific age and helmet requirements. 
• E-bikes are required to display a classification label under state law. 
• Dirt bikes generally cannot be operated on public roads and must be used on private property with permission.
